title: "Survey Mode, Undecided Voters and Polling Error in the 2012 and 2016 U.S. Presidential Elections"
author:
  - "Caitlin Knowles (a1993232)"
  - "Isobel Cusack (a1971531)"
  - "Linh Chi Nguyen (a1954861)"

date: today

abstract: |
 This report investigates how survey mode and reported undecided voter share were associated with polling error in the 2012 and 2016 U.S. presidential elections, while accounting for the number of days before Election Day. Using polling data from HuffPost Pollster/rOpenGov and official electoral results from the MIT Election Data and Science Lab, the analysis evaluates 1,219 polls ending within 90 days of the elections. Absolute polling error was calculated by comparing the Democratic–Republican polling margin with the actual election margin. Multiple linear regression models were fitted using the square root of absolute polling error to examine associations with polling method and undecided voter share, and whether these associations differed between the two election periods. The results suggested that the difference between Internet and Live Phone polls changed between the two elections, while there was not enough evidence that the association with undecided voter share differed by year. These findings should be interpreted with caution because polls from the same state or pollster may not be independent.

**Code and data:** all analysis for this report is reproducible from the repository at <https://github.com/statprac/Final-Report.git> <!-- See rubric: Code repository -->

```{r}
#| label: setup

library(tidyverse)
library(modelsummary)
library(knitr)

# Load the final analysis dataset
analysis <- read_csv(
  "project datasets/analysis_data_final.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

# Use the same reference groups as in the analysis script
analysis <- analysis |>
  mutate(
    year = factor(year, levels = c(2012, 2016)),
    mode = factor(mode, levels = c("Live Phone", "Internet", "IVR/Online"))
  )

# Fit the models before they are used in Results
model_sqrt_additive <- lm(
  sqrt(absolute_error) ~ Undecided + days_to_election + mode + year,
  data = analysis
)
model_sqrt <- lm(
  sqrt(absolute_error) ~ year * (Undecided + days_to_election + mode),
  data = analysis
)
```

# Introduction {#sec-intro}

Pre-electoral polling plays an important role in understanding the public's political opinions and stances during election periods and can assist in predicting the outcomes of elections [@traugott_2005]. Polling on a state level is particularly insightful in the United States, as the results are determined by the Electoral College as opposed to national popular vote or preferential voting [@soumbatiants_chappell_johnson_2006]. Relative support for candidates on a state level can be estimated through polls, which can help assess how competitive each individual electoral contest is [@soumbatiants_chappell_johnson_2006]. While polling is an insightful tool, it does not always accurately reflect the final results of elections [@traugott_2005]. This is why it is important to understand what factors are associated with discrepancies between actual voting outcomes and polling estimates.

This analysis focuses on two polling features that may be associated with polling error: the proportion of undecided voters and the survey mode used to obtain responses. Only polls within 90 days of the elections will be considered. The reported share of undecided voters may increase uncertainty as to which party/candidate is more likely to win prior to the election. Similarly, survey mode may be associated with differences in polling accuracy. Comparing 2012 and 2016 election polls and results allows the investigation of whether associations between polling error and polling characteristics are consistent across election periods. Previous research suggests that undecided voters are important when evaluating election polls. Bon and colleagues examined U.S. presidential elections from 2004 to 2016 and found that the allocation of undecided voters could contribute to polling bias, particularly in 2016 [@bon_ballard_baffour_2018]. This provides a reason to investigate whether reported undecided voter share is associated with polling error in our data. This analysis investigates how survey mode and reported undecided voter share are associated with state-level polling error, after accounting for time before Election Day, and whether these associations differ between the 2012 and 2016 elections.

# Method {#sec-method}

## Data

This study used three datasets: state-level presidential polling data from the 2012 and 2016 U.S. elections, obtained through the HuffPost Pollster/rOpenGov collection [@arnold_leeper_linzer], and presidential election results from the MIT Election Data and Science Lab (MEDSL) [@mit_election_data_and_science_lab_2017]. The polling datasets contained 1,135 records from 2012 and 1,303 from 2016. Each polling record was treated as one observation.

The election results were restricted to 2012 and 2016 and used to calculate actual state-level Democratic–Republican vote margins.

The variables used in the final analysis are summarised in @tbl-descriptives.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-descriptives
#| tbl-cap: "Summary of numerical variables in the final analysis sample."

library(tidyverse)
library(knitr)

analysis_data <- read_csv(
  "project datasets/analysis_data_final.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

analysis_data |>
  select(absolute_error, Undecided, days_to_election) |>
  pivot_longer(
    everything(),
    names_to = "Variable",
    values_to = "Value"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    Variable = case_when(
      Variable == "absolute_error" ~ "Absolute polling error (percentage points)",
      Variable == "Undecided" ~ "Undecided voter share (%)",
      Variable == "days_to_election" ~ "Days before Election Day")
  ) |>
  group_by(Variable) |>
  summarise(
    Mean = mean(Value, na.rm = TRUE),
    SD = sd(Value, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  kable(digits = 2, col.names = c("Variable", "Mean", "SD"))
```

## Data Preparation and Sample Selection

The initial cleaning of the polling data was completed for the
[EDA report](https://github.com/statprac/EDA-report/blob/master/EDA-report.qmd).
The corresponding [cleaning script](https://github.com/statprac/EDA-report/blob/master/clean-poll-data.R)
is also available in the EDA repository.

The 2012 and 2016 polling datasets were combined after standardising state names, election years and polling dates to ensure consistency. Official election results were then matched to the polling data by state and year. Before calculating actual election margins, votes received by the same major-party candidate under different party labels were combined to avoid underestimating their total support.

The analysis was restricted to polls ending between 90 days before Election Day and Election Day itself. This period was selected to focus on polls conducted closer to the election. Records with missing or non-positive sample sizes, unavailable polling errors or missing undecided voter shares were excluded, leaving 1,561 observations at this stage. Missing undecided values were not replaced with zero because missing information does not necessarily indicate that no respondents were undecided.

The primary analysis focused on Live Phone, Internet and IVR/Online polls, reducing the sample to 1,221 observations. These three survey modes were selected because they were represented in both election years, allowing comparisons of their relationships with polling error. Other modes were excluded because they had limited representation or were not available consistently across both years.

Finally, two polls for which the sum of reported response percentages exceeded 102% were excluded from the main analysis, leaving 1,219 polls. The number of polls remaining after each selection step is shown in @tbl-sample-selection. As these totals do not necessarily indicate errors, both polls were included in a sensitivity analysis to assess whether their exclusion affected the results.

### Variable construction

Polling accuracy was measured using the absolute difference between the reported Democratic–Republican polling margin and the actual election margin.

The polling margin was calculated as:

$$
\text{Poll margin}
= \text{Democratic poll percentage} - \text{Republican poll percentage}
$$

The actual election margin was calculated as:

$$
\text{Actual margin}
= \frac{\text{Democratic votes} - \text{Republican votes}}
       {\text{Total votes}}
  \times 100
$$

Absolute polling error was then defined as:

$$
\text{Absolute error}
= \left| \text{Poll margin} - \text{Actual margin} \right|
$$

A lower absolute error indicates greater polling accuracy. All margins and errors were expressed in percentage points.

The main explanatory variables were reported undecided voter share and survey mode. Undecided voter share was measured as a percentage. Days before Election Day was calculated from each poll's end date, while election year distinguished the 2012 and 2016 observations.

The variables used in the analysis are described in @tbl-variables.

| Variable | Description |
|---|---|
| Absolute polling error | Absolute difference between the Democratic–Republican polling margin and the actual election margin, in percentage points. |
| Undecided voter share | Percentage of poll respondents reported as undecided. |
| Survey mode | Method used to conduct the poll: Live Phone, Internet or IVR/Online. |
| Days before Election Day | Number of days between the poll's end date and Election Day. |
| Election year | Year of the election: 2012 or 2016. |

: Variables used in the analysis and what they represent. {#tbl-variables}

## Statistical methods

Multiple linear regression was used to examine associations with polling error and whether these differed by year.

The response variable was the square root of absolute polling error. This transformation was chosen after comparing diagnostic plots for models using the original error, $\log(1 + \text{absolute error})$, and the square root of the error. Each poll was given equal weight in the regression. Election year and survey mode were treated as categorical variables, with 2012 and Live Phone as the reference groups.

An additive model and an interaction model were fitted using the square-root-transformed response. The additive model assumed that the associations between the explanatory variables and polling error were the same in both years. The interaction model allowed the associations of survey mode, undecided voter percentage and days before the election with polling error to differ by year. The two nested models were compared using an F-test. The model comparison is provided in @tbl-app-model-comparison. The final model was selected by considering the research question, model comparison and diagnostic plots.

Residuals against fitted values and a Scale–Location plot were examined to assess the model form and the spread of residuals. A normal Q–Q plot was used to assess residual normality, and Cook’s distance was used to identify potentially influential observations. Generalised variance inflation factors were also examined to assess possible multicollinearity among predictor terms. The diagnostic plots for the final model are shown in @fig-diagnostics.

The square-root transformation was selected because the Q–Q plot was closer to a straight line than for the models using the original and log-transformed responses, while the spread of residuals was reasonably consistent. 

A sensitivity analysis was conducted by refitting the final model after adding back the two polls with unusual reported response totals. The estimated coefficients were compared with and without these polls. The coefficient comparison is provided in @tbl-app-sensitivity. Because polls from the same state or pollster may not be independent, the usual confidence intervals and p-values are interpreted with caution.

# Results {#sec-results}

Using linear regression, the associations of year, percentage of undecided voters, number of days to the election and mode of polling with the square root of absolute polling error are described by the following model:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\widehat{E}[\sqrt{\text{Error}_i}\mid X_i] ={}&
\hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1 Y_i + \hat\beta_2 U_i + \hat\beta_3 D_i \\
&+ \hat\beta_4 I_i + \hat\beta_5 V_i
+ \hat\beta_6(Y_i U_i) + \hat\beta_7(Y_i D_i) \\
&+ \hat\beta_8(Y_i I_i) + \hat\beta_9(Y_i V_i).
\end{aligned}
$$

Here, $Y_i$ indicates 2016, $U_i$ is the reported undecided voter percentage, $D_i$ is days before the election, and $I_i$ and $V_i$ indicate Internet and IVR/Online polls, respectively. The estimated coefficients and their 95% confidence intervals are reported in @tbl-model-detail.

The coefficient for `year2016` was statistically significant under the usual model assumptions (p = 0.0000966). Because the model includes interactions, this coefficient represents the difference between years for Live Phone polls when undecided voter share and days before the election are both zero. It should therefore not be interpreted as an overall difference between the two election years.

The `year2016:modeInternet` coefficient was also statistically significant under the usual model assumptions ($p \approx 0.00259$). This suggests that the difference between Internet and Live Phone polls changed between 2012 and 2016. In 2012, the estimated Internet coefficient relative to Live Phone was −0.198, while in 2016 the combined coefficient was approximately 0.178. These coefficients are on the square-root scale.

For undecided voter share, the estimated coefficient was 0.0273 in 2012 and approximately 0.0040 in 2016. The interaction between undecided voter share and year was not statistically significant ($p \approx 0.193$), so there was not enough evidence to conclude that the association differed between the two years.

@fig-mode-predictions shows the predicted mean of the square-root-transformed error for each mode and year, holding undecided voter share at 5% and days before the election at 26. The usual 95% confidence intervals should be interpreted cautiously because polls may not be independent.

![Predicted mean of the square root of absolute polling error by survey mode and year, with usual 95% confidence intervals, at 5% undecided voters and 26 days before Election Day. The estimated difference between Internet and Live Phone changes direction between years.](survey_mode_predictions.png){#fig-mode-predictions}


The model comparison in @tbl-app-model-comparison provided some support for including the year interactions as a group (F = 3.068, p = 0.0158). As polls may not be independent, the F-test and individual p-values should be interpreted with caution. The final model explained approximately 11.8% of the variation in the square-root-transformed absolute polling error.

## Checking assumptions
```{r}
#| label: fig-diagnostics
#| fig-cap: "Residuals versus fitted values, normal Q-Q, Scale-Location and residuals versus leverage for the final square-root model. The Q-Q plot departs from the line at the tails, and the Scale-Location plot suggests a slight increase in residual spread."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 7
#| echo: false
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(model_sqrt)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

**Linearity:** Residuals were distributed around zero, with no strong curved pattern in the Residuals vs Fitted plot. There was no clear evidence of a major departure from the assumed model form.

**Normality:** The points in the normal Q–Q plot show that the residuals lie mostly close to the straight line in the middle, with departures at either end. Therefore, the residuals are not perfectly normally distributed.

**Homoscedasticity:** The trend-line of the Scale–Location plot is reasonably flat over part of its range, although it also suggests a slight increase in spread. Therefore, the assumption of constant variance may not be fully satisfied.

**Independence:** Independence of observations is difficult to determine. Polls from the same pollster or state may be related, which may affect the assumption of independence. The unequal number of polls in 2012 (402) and 2016 (817) is also relevant when comparing the two elections. Possible dependence between polls may affect standard errors, confidence intervals and p-values.

Using variance inflation factors and looking at $GVIF^{1/(2 \times Df)}$ shows that the reported values fall below $\sqrt{5}$. The adjusted GVIF takes account of differing degrees of freedom. The highest reported adjusted value is for `days_to_election` at 1.380; the full results are provided in @tbl-app-vif. These values do not indicate a strong multicollinearity concern under this reference threshold, although they do not prove that multicollinearity is absent.

**Cook’s distance:** The largest Cook’s distance was approximately 0.014, as shown in @tbl-app-cooks. The five observations with the largest values were inspected and retained because there was no clear reason to remove them. All five were from 2012, across different states, pollsters and polling modes.

### Sensitivity analysis

Including the two unusual polls led to small changes in the estimated coefficients on the square-root scale. The largest change was an increase of 0.0169 for `year2016:modeIVR/Online`; all coefficient estimates retained the same sign. The full comparison is shown in @tbl-app-sensitivity.

# Discussion

The results suggest that the association between survey mode and polling error differed between the two elections, particularly for Internet polls compared with Live Phone polls. However, there was not enough evidence to conclude that the association between undecided voter share and polling error differed between the two years.

The estimated association between undecided voter share and polling error was smaller in 2016 than in 2012, but there was not enough evidence that it differed between years. This does not mean that undecided voters are unimportant.

Previous research by Bon and colleagues found that undecided voters were important when examining polling bias, particularly in the 2016 election [@bon_ballard_baffour_2018]. Their study focused on polling bias and the allocation of undecided voters, while this investigation examined the size of absolute polling error. The studies also used different models and selection periods, so the results are not directly comparable.

Survey mode also differed in its association with polling error between election periods. In 2012, IVR/Online and Internet polls had negative coefficients in relation to Live Phone polls. In 2016, the combined coefficient for Internet relative to Live Phone was positive, whereas the coefficient for IVR/Online relative to Live Phone remained negative. The Internet-by-year interaction provided evidence that the difference between Internet and Live Phone polls changed between the two elections under the usual model assumptions. However, the results do not establish that a particular survey mode consistently causes polls to be more accurate.

The sensitivity analysis showed that the coefficient estimates changed after the two unusual polls were added back, although the estimated directions remained the same. The sensitivity analysis compared estimates, rather than confidence intervals or p-values.

## Limitations

The analysis performed identifies associations between predictors and response variables; this does not mean there is necessarily a causal relationship in the data. Other factors may also be associated with polling error. Polls with missing undecided voter shares were excluded, which may cause selection bias if such polls differ systematically from those that were included in the final dataset. In this investigation, only three survey modes were included; therefore, the associations found cannot be generalised to other survey modes. Polls from the same state and polling organisation could be related, which can affect the reliability of standard errors, confidence intervals and p-values, as the observations may not be independent. The diagnostic plots also showed departures from normality at the tails and a slight increase in residual spread, so the model assumptions were not fully satisfied. Finally, only two election periods were covered in this analysis, meaning that the findings may not be applicable to all elections, particularly historical elections that would not have used the same polling methods. It was also chosen to only analyse polls within a 90-day period of the election; it should be considered that associations may differ for polls outside of this period. The final model explained a relatively small proportion of the variation in the square-root-transformed polling error, so the included variables alone do not explain most of the variation in the selected polls.

# Statistical appendix {#sec-appendix}

This appendix documents the data preparation, model comparison, diagnostics and sensitivity analysis. The analysis uses the cleaned polling data from the EDA and the election results in the project repository.

The full code for data preparation and sensitivity analysis is available in
[data_preparation.R](https://github.com/statprac/Final-Report/blob/main/project%20datasets/data_preparation.R).
The modelling and diagnostic code is available in
[model_analysis.R](https://github.com/statprac/Final-Report/blob/main/model_analysis.R).

## Data preparation and sample selection {#sec-app-data}

The data preparation code constructs the poll and election margins, identifies unusual reported totals and applies the sample selection rules. Missing response categories are ignored when calculating the reported total. The two unusual polls are excluded from `main_data` and retained in `sensitivity_data`.

```{r}
#| label: app-data-preparation
#| echo: false
#| results: hide
# Data preparation and sensitivity check

library(tidyverse)

# 1. Read the combined cleaned polling data and election results.
polls <- read_csv(
  "project datasets/clean/state_polls_combined_clean.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)
elections <- read_csv(
  "project datasets/raw/1976-2024-president.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

# Check that each state-poll has a unique identifier.
sum(is.na(polls$poll_key)) # Count missing poll keys

sum(duplicated(polls$poll_key)) # Count duplicate poll keys

# 2. Count each major candidate's votes across all party labels.
# This includes votes reported on extra ballot lines, especially in New York.
elections <- elections |>
  filter(year %in% c(2012, 2016)) |>
  mutate(
    state = str_replace_all(str_to_lower(state), " ", "-"),
    state = if_else(state == "district-of-columbia", "washington-dc", state),
    candidate_group = case_when(
      year == 2012 & candidate == "OBAMA, BARACK H." ~ "Democrat",
      year == 2012 & candidate == "ROMNEY, MITT" ~ "Republican",
      year == 2016 & candidate == "CLINTON, HILLARY" ~ "Democrat",
      year == 2016 & candidate == "TRUMP, DONALD J." ~ "Republican",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    )
  )

# Check Democrat and Republican records with no candidate name
unknown_candidate <- elections |>
  filter(
    is.na(candidate),
    party_simplified %in% c("DEMOCRAT", "REPUBLICAN")
  ) |>
  select(year, state, party_simplified, candidatevotes)

print(unknown_candidate)

# Each state-year should have one total-votes value.
vote_totals <- elections |>
  group_by(year, state) |>
  summarise(total_votes = first(totalvotes),
            number_of_totals = n_distinct(totalvotes), .groups = "drop")

# Count state-year records with different total-vote values
print(sum(vote_totals$number_of_totals != 1))

# Count state-year records with missing total votes
print(sum(is.na(vote_totals$total_votes)))

# Count state-year records with zero or negative total votes
print(sum(vote_totals$total_votes <= 0, na.rm = TRUE))

candidate_votes <- elections |>
  filter(!is.na(candidate_group)) |>
  group_by(year, state, candidate_group) |>
  summarise(votes = sum(candidatevotes), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = candidate_group, values_from = votes)

actual_results <- candidate_votes |>
  left_join(vote_totals, by = c("year", "state")) |>
  mutate(actual_margin = 100 * (Democrat - Republican) / total_votes) |>
  select(year, state, actual_margin)

# Count duplicate state-year election results
print(sum(duplicated(actual_results[c("year", "state")])))

# Count missing actual margins
print(sum(is.na(actual_results$actual_margin)))

# 3. Join each poll to its state-year election result.
polls <- polls |>
  left_join(actual_results, by = c("year", "state")) |>
  mutate(
    poll_margin = case_when(
      year == 2012 ~ Obama - Romney,
      year == 2016 ~ Clinton - Trump
    ),
    absolute_error = abs(poll_margin - actual_margin)
  )
# Count polls without a matching election result
print(sum(is.na(polls$actual_margin)))

# 4. Flag polls whose reported response percentages add to more than 102%.
# Missing categories are ignored when adding reported values.
# A high total may reflect rounding or reporting differences, so we do not indicate that it is an error.
polls <- polls |>
  mutate(
    reported_total = case_when(
      year == 2012 ~ rowSums(across(c(Obama, Romney, Undecided, Other)), na.rm = TRUE),
      year == 2016 ~ rowSums(across(c(Clinton, Trump, Undecided, Other, Johnson, McMullin)), na.rm = TRUE)
    ),
    unusual_total = reported_total > 102
  )

# 5. Select polls from the final 90 days.
# Exclude polls with missing or non-positive sample size.
# After data exploration, we agree to include 3 modes: Live Phone, Internet and IVR/Online polls into the model. 
# Furthermore, we exclude the two flagged polls from the main sample
# and include them in a sensitivity check.

sample_90 <- polls |> filter(between(days_to_election, 0, 90))
valid <- sample_90 |>
  filter(!is.na(absolute_error), !is.na(sample_size), sample_size > 0)
# Polls that do not report undecided share are excluded; this may affect results.
complete <- valid |> filter(!is.na(Undecided))
selected <- complete |>
  filter(mode %in% c("Live Phone", "Internet", "IVR/Online")) |>
  mutate(
    year = factor(year, levels = c(2012, 2016)),
    mode = factor(mode, levels = c("Live Phone", "Internet", "IVR/Online"))
  )

main_data <- selected |> filter(!unusual_total)
sensitivity_data <- selected
unusual_records <- selected |>
  filter(unusual_total) |>
  select(poll_key, year, state, pollster, mode,
         Obama, Romney, Clinton, Trump, Undecided, Johnson, McMullin, Other,
         reported_total)

sample_counts <- tibble(
  stage = c("Cleaned polls", "Within 90 days", "Valid error and sample size",
            "Undecided reported", "Three modes", "Main sample"),
  remaining = c(nrow(polls), nrow(sample_90), nrow(valid), nrow(complete),
                nrow(selected), nrow(main_data))
) |>
  mutate(excluded_at_step = lag(remaining) - remaining)

print(sample_counts)
print(unusual_records, width = Inf)
print(table(main_data$year, main_data$mode))
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sample-selection
#| tbl-cap: "Polls remaining after each selection step. The main analysis included 1,219 polls."
#| echo: false
knitr::kable(sample_counts)
```

## Model comparison and final model {#sec-app-model}

The additive and interaction models were fitted on the square-root scale. Their comparison tests the year interactions as a group. Reference groups are 2012 and Live Phone.

```{r}
#| label: app-fit-models
#| echo: false
# Fit the additive and interaction models to the same sample
model_sqrt_additive <- lm(
  sqrt(absolute_error) ~ Undecided + days_to_election + mode + year,
  data = main_data
)
model_sqrt <- lm(
  sqrt(absolute_error) ~ year * (Undecided + days_to_election + mode),
  data = main_data
)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-app-model-comparison
#| tbl-cap: "Comparison of additive and interaction models on the square-root scale. The F-test compares the year interactions as a group."
#| echo: false
model_comparison <- anova(model_sqrt_additive, model_sqrt)
rownames(model_comparison) <- c("Additive model", "Interaction model")
knitr::kable(model_comparison, digits = 3, row.names = TRUE)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-model-detail
#| tbl-cap: "Final model coefficients, 95% confidence intervals and p-values on the square-root scale. The reference groups are 2012 and Live Phone."
#| echo: false
model_results <- data.frame(
  Estimate = coef(model_sqrt),
  confint(model_sqrt),
  p_value = format.pval(
    coef(summary(model_sqrt))[, "Pr(>|t|)"],
    digits = 3,
    eps = 0.001
  ),
  check.names = FALSE
)
knitr::kable(model_results, digits = 3)
```

## Diagnostic checks {#sec-app-checks}

The final-model diagnostic plots in @fig-diagnostics examine residual patterns, normality, residual spread and influential observations.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-app-vif
#| tbl-cap: "Generalised variance inflation factors for predictors and their interaction terms."
#| echo: false

# Check predictor groups with their interaction terms
vif_results <- car::vif(model_sqrt, type = "predictor")
knitr::kable(
  vif_results[, c("GVIF", "Df", "GVIF^(1/(2*Df))")],
  digits = 3
)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-app-cooks
#| tbl-cap: "Five polls with the largest Cook's distances in the final model. The largest Cook's distance was approximately 0.014."
#| echo: false
# Inspect the polls with the largest Cook's distances
cook_values <- cooks.distance(model_sqrt)
top_polls <- head(order(cook_values, decreasing = TRUE), 5)
main_data |>
  slice(top_polls) |>
  select(year, state, pollster, mode, absolute_error) |>
  mutate(Cooks_distance = cook_values[top_polls]) |>
  knitr::kable(
    digits = 3,
    col.names = c("Year", "State", "Pollster", "Mode", "Error", "Cook's D")
  )
```

## Sensitivity analysis {#sec-app-sensitivity}

The same final model was refitted after adding the two unusual polls. Estimates are compared on the square-root scale.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-app-sensitivity
#| tbl-cap: "Sensitivity analysis on the square-root scale. Change is the estimate including the two unusual polls minus the main-sample estimate."
#| echo: false
model_with_unusual <- lm(
  sqrt(absolute_error) ~ year * (Undecided + days_to_election + mode),
  data = sensitivity_data
)

# Compare matching coefficient estimates
sensitivity_comparison <- tibble(
  Term = names(coef(model_sqrt)),
  Main_sample = unname(coef(model_sqrt)),
  With_unusual = unname(coef(model_with_unusual))
) |>
  mutate(Change = With_unusual - Main_sample)
knitr::kable(sensitivity_comparison, digits = 5)
```

The ordinary confidence intervals and F-test assume independent observations. Polls from the same state or pollster may be related, so these results should be interpreted with caution.
